summary.text: Animal behaviour is the individual or social behaviour of animals that contributes to their survival, and it is studied by the science of ethology.
Behaviour is determined by three major factors: inborn instincts, learning, and environmental factors.
Animals learn in several ways, including habituation, associative learning and imprinting.

facts.label: Associative learning pioneer
facts.value: Ivan Pavlov, using dogs and a bell

facts.label: Imprinting timing
facts.value: Only in a very limited period of time

facts.label: Social transmission example
facts.value: Potato cleaning spread among Hachijojima macaques

items.prompt: Prairie dogs living beside a hiking trail stop diving into burrows every time someone walks past. What is happening?

options.label: They have lost the ability to hear the hikers
They are copying the hikers' calm behaviour
They have learned to ignore a stimulus that does not matter
They have formed a bond with the first hiker they saw

items.explain: Habituation is the process by which an animal learns not to respond to irrelevant stimuli, which saves time and energy.

items.prompt: A dog starts drooling at the sound of a dinner bell before any food appears. What kind of learning is this?

options.label: Associative learning, where a new response links to a stimulus
Imprinting, which takes place only in an early period
Habituation, where the dog stops reacting to the bell
Imitation, where the dog copies another dog

items.explain: In associative learning a new response becomes associated with a particular stimulus, as in Pavlov's dogs that salivated at a bell.

items.prompt: Goslings hatched in an incubator follow a researcher's boots as if they were their mother. When must the boots have been presented?

options.label: At any point during the goslings' first year
During a critical period of a few days after hatching
Only after the goslings had seen their mother
Only before the goslings had hatched

items.explain: Imprinting takes place only in a limited period; the response can be imitated by an arbitrary stimulus presented during a critical period lasting a few days after hatching.

items.prompt: A newly hatched chick has never seen a parent feed anything, yet it makes beak movements that prompt the parent to give it food. What best explains this?

options.label: Associative learning from earlier meals
Imitation of its older siblings
Habituation to its parent's presence
An inborn fixed action pattern, set off by a stimulus

items.explain: Fixed action patterns are instinctive sequences that happen without learning; the beak movements of newly hatched chicks are a well-studied example.

items.prompt: A monkey watches another monkey handle a rope, becomes curious about the rope, and later succeeds by its own method after trial and error. What is this?

options.label: Observational learning through stimulus enhancement, not imitation
Imitation, since it copied every move exactly
Imprinting during a critical period
A fixed action pattern set off by a releaser

items.explain: Interest in an object after watching others lets an animal learn new behaviours by trial and error without imitating; the observer in the experiment used a different method.

items.prompt: One macaque starts cleaning potatoes in the sea, and soon the animals around her do it too, as do their young. What is this an example of?

options.label: A fixed action pattern set off by a clear releaser
Imprinting during a critical period after hatching
Social transmission of a behaviour through contact within the group
Habituation to humans who walk along the beach

items.explain: The potato-cleaning habit spread to individuals in contact with the first macaque and to their young, a form of social transmission.

pack.title: Born Knowing, or Learned?
pack.question: Where does an animal's behaviour come from?

beats.title: Born Knowing, or Learned?
beats.hook: A chick taps its parent's beak the day it hatches, while a prairie dog learns to ignore hikers.

beats.prompt: A newly hatched chick has never seen a parent feed anything, yet it makes beak movements that lead the parent to give it food. Where does the movement come from?
beats.explain: The beak movements of newly hatched chicks are a well-studied fixed action pattern, an instinctive sequence that does not depend on learning.

choices.label: It formed an association between beak movements and food, as Pavlov's dogs did
choices.feedback: Association needs repeated experience, and a newly hatched chick has none yet.

choices.label: It learned the movement by watching its siblings
choices.feedback: It tempts because learning is common, but a newly hatched chick has had no time to learn this.

choices.label: It is an inborn fixed action pattern, set off by a stimulus

beats.prompt: Match each researcher to the behaviour they studied.

right.label: Young geese following a stimulus in a critical period

beats.explain: Each researcher is tied to a classic study of learning or instinct in animals.

beats.prompt: Sort each behaviour by whether it is an instinct or learned.

left.label: Pavlov's dogs drooling at a bell

beats.explain: Fixed action patterns such as beak movements and the waggle dance are instincts, while habituation, associative learning and imprinting are forms of learning.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong. Which?

steps.text: Prairie dogs give alarm calls when predators approach.
Near a human trail, calling every time someone passes costs time and energy.
Over time they learn not to respond to these irrelevant stimuli.
So habituation means the prairie dogs lose the ability to give alarm calls.

beats.explain: Habituation means the animal ceases responding to a stimulus it has learned is irrelevant; it does not remove the ability to respond.

beats.idea: Behaviour is determined by inborn instincts, learning and environmental factors working together.

paragraphs.heading: What shapes behaviour
paragraphs.text: Animal behaviour is what animals do, alone or in groups, that helps them survive, and the science that studies it is called ethology. Three main things shape it: instincts an animal is born with, learning, and the environment. The environment includes non-living factors such as temperature and light, which matter a lot for ectothermic or nocturnal animals. It also includes living factors such as members of the same species, predators, parasites and disease.

paragraphs.heading: Instincts that run to the end
paragraphs.text: Konrad Lorenz made fixed action patterns famous, though the idea probably owes more to his teacher, Oskar Heinroth. A fixed action pattern is an inborn chain of actions that is much the same across a species and nearly always runs to completion once started. The stimulus that sets it off is called a releaser. A well-known case is the beak movements of newly hatched chicks, which prompt the mother to bring up food for them.

paragraphs.heading: Learning to ignore
paragraphs.text: Habituation is a simple kind of learning seen in many groups of animals: the animal stops responding to a stimulus that does not matter. Prairie dogs, for example, give alarm calls when predators come near, and the whole group dashes into burrows. Near trails used by people, calling every time a person walks past would waste time and energy. So getting used to humans is an important behaviour for these prairie dogs.

paragraphs.heading: Bells and baby geese
paragraphs.text: In associative learning, a new response gets linked to a particular stimulus. Ivan Pavlov showed this when dogs trained to connect food with a bell began to salivate at the sound of the bell. Imprinting is another kind of learning that lets young animals recognise their own species, and it can only happen in a short window of time. Lorenz saw that young geese and chickens follow their mothers almost from the day they hatch. He found that if the eggs were hatched artificially, an arbitrary stimulus shown during a critical period of a few days after hatching could call up the same response.

paragraphs.heading: Copying others
paragraphs.text: Imitation means watching another animal and repeating exactly what it does. Capuchin monkeys preferred researchers who imitated them, spending more time with them and choosing to do tasks with them. Chimpanzees, given the choice, preferred to copy an older, higher-ranking chimp over a younger, lower-ranking one.

paragraphs.heading: Potatoes washed in the sea
paragraphs.text: A famous case of a behaviour spreading socially comes from macaques on Hachijojima Island in Japan. In the 1960s researchers started leaving potatoes on the beach, and the monkeys soon came out of the forest to pick them from the sand and clean them. About a year later, one monkey began washing her potato in the sea. Those around her picked up the habit, and their young did too.
